accepted.title: Treating postoperative DVT during prophylaxis

record.title: Treating postoperative DVT during prophylaxis
fairness: Therapeutic enoxaparin is the best offered plan: interpret the noncompressible femoral vein as proximal DVT, then distinguish prophylaxis and minor stable wound spotting from therapeutic failure or a major bleeding contraindication. Continuing prevention undertreats the event; the represented bleeding does not justify withholding treatment for a filter.

High-yield two-step treatment decision, although the minor-spotting alternative limits difficulty. The standalone update supplies the returned study and medication/bleeding record. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Report scope: all 29 active candidate nodes were independently reviewed, including active original drafts preserved after review one. Five original Keep records, retired/superseded histories, 17 parked drafts, five historical hold/drop records and three unkeyed planning slots were noted but not scored. Only candidate visible text determines findings; author assertions and prior PASS labels do not. This offline editorial review does not freshly verify sources or exact guideline thresholds and is not clinical approval.
suggestions: Retain the prophylaxis indication and actual bleeding trend; these are necessary clinical data.
Optional cleanup: shorten the obsolete outside-scan history now that the task begins with a complete hospital duplex.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 62-year-old man, attends clinic after colectomy for diverticulitis. His left calf and thigh have become swollen and tender. An outside report says no thrombosis. The acquisition log lists compressible posterior tibial and peroneal veins; its femoral and popliteal fields are marked not acquired. His foot is warm and moving normally.
after.Current update: The hospital's complete duplex now records a noncompressible left femoral vein. The medication administration record lists enoxaparin under postoperative prevention. A small blood spot appeared during one dressing change; the incision remains closed, drain output is serous and repeated hemoglobin values are stable. Renal function is stable.
after.Task: Which initial treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s returned study and medication record?
Options: **KEY:** Start therapeutic enoxaparin treatment
Withhold enoxaparin and insert a retrievable IVC filter
Continue the postoperative prevention prescription

accepted.explanation: The new proximal finding needs treatment; the prior prevention prescription does not establish therapeutic failure. The represented wound/laboratory trajectory does not establish a major bleeding contraindication that requires a routine filter. Minor stable wound spotting is not the active major-bleeding contraindication that would support this temporary-protection pathway. Misreading it can withhold needed proximal-DVT treatment.

accepted.title: Provoked DVT duration with heterozygous factor V Leiden

record.title: Provoked DVT duration with heterozygous factor V Leiden
fairness: Stopping at the completed three-month course is the best offered plan for the first DVT after major benign surgery with recovery. Isolated heterozygous factor V Leiden does not automatically require indefinite therapy.

Two consequential steps: establish that the provoking exposure has resolved, then decide whether the genetic result changes management. Indefinite treatment is a credible overreaction; arbitrary six-month extension is weaker. High-yield and moderate.

The explicit three-month update supplies the later clinical state without a preceding node. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; exact guideline duration and thrombophilia recommendations were not freshly verified offline.
suggestions: Optional presentation cleanup: frame this as a three-month follow-up and put the acute swelling history in past tense.
Preserve the benign surgical indication, recovered mobility, first-event status and exact heterozygous result; do not generalize to all thrombophilias.

after.Presentation: {patientName}, a 62-year-old man, attends clinic after colectomy for diverticulitis with new left calf and thigh swelling. The outside ultrasound log lists compression images of posterior tibial and peroneal veins, which flatten under the probe. Its separate common-femoral Doppler recordings vary with respiration on both sides. No other compression images are listed.
after.Current update: Hospital duplex documented a femoral DVT five days after the colectomy, and {patientName} has received therapeutic anticoagulation for three months. The operation was for diverticulitis. His wound has healed and he walks and works at his usual level. This was his first VTE. An outside genetic result, obtained earlier, reports heterozygous factor V Leiden.
after.Task: Which anticoagulation-duration plan best fits {patientName} at this three-month review?
Options: **KEY:** Stop anticoagulation at this review
Continue anticoagulation for indefinite secondary prevention
Continue anticoagulation for six additional months

accepted.explanation: The event followed major benign surgery and the observed recovery removes that transient exposure. Isolated heterozygous factor V Leiden does not by itself convert this first provoked event into an indication for indefinite therapy. A positive inherited test is not automatically a high-risk persistent thrombophilia. The cited guide separates isolated heterozygous factor V Leiden from higher-risk thrombophilic states; the represented episode and recovery support a finite course.

record.title: Persistently abnormal fistula maturation examination
fairness: Duplex characterization before use is the best offered plan. Visible enlargement does not establish usability when serial thrill, pulsatility and elevation findings remain abnormal.

The presentation gives actual examination findings and chronology rather than an immature-fistula label. Complete standalone context; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

accepted.title: Acute multinerve deficit after fistula creation

record.title: Acute multinerve deficit after fistula creation
fairness: Immediate vascular assessment for access ligation is the best offered response to severe acute pain with multinerve motor/sensory deficits despite a warm hand and pulse. The resolved regional block and soft forearm address important competitors.

Two consequential steps: localize beyond a single median entrapment, then recognize that preserved gross perfusion does not exclude urgent access-related neurologic injury. High-yield and moderate rather than hard because the competitors become weak once the pattern is recognized.

The retrospective admission frame and decision point are clear and self-contained. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the plan correctly requests urgent assessment rather than claiming a procedure has occurred.
suggestions: Keep the warm-hand/pulse findings as the meaningful counterweight.
Do not present waiting for formal electrodiagnostic confirmation as an equivalent safe pathway for this acute deficit.

after.Task: Which plan best fits that point in {patientName}'s outside postoperative record?

accepted.title: Recurrent symptoms after achalasia treatment: next investigation

record.title: Recurrent symptoms after achalasia treatment: next investigation
fairness: Timed barium esophagography with tablet passage is the best offered next investigation for recurrent obstructive symptoms after treatment of established achalasia. The indication for POEM is explicit in the candidate itself; no earlier node or inferred diagnosis is needed. The complete task asks for the next investigation and all three options answer that task.

The two consequential steps are to recognize that technically adequate, reassuring pressure measurements do not establish adequate bolus emptying, then prioritize an objective clearance study despite the competing possibility of post-POEM reflux. Upper endoscopy remains a credible complementary investigation for mucosal disease or narrowing; the explanation appropriately does not claim maintained weight and hydration exclude those conditions. Reflux monitoring does not resolve the immediate clearance question. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in these supplied fields; the guideline ranking was assessed offline and was not independently reverified against a current source.

Cover-the-key attack: 'achalasia treated with POEM' is legitimate established history for this management question, not disclosure of a requested diagnosis. 'relaxation within the laboratory interval' supplies the potentially misleading observation the resident must interpret, rather than announcing that emptying is normal. 'food again pauses and fluid returns at night' keeps retention and reflux in competition. None of those phrases lexically selects one option without clinical knowledge. The investigation labels have comparable specificity and no unique qualifier, rhetorical absolute, conspicuously long key, convergence pattern or pre-answer teaching sentence.

This is a high-yield assessment of recurrent symptoms after definitive achalasia treatment. Predicted difficulty is moderate, not hard: a resident who recalls the post-treatment investigation recommendation may answer directly, but the normal manometry and reflux-like symptom create credible competing errors. Difficulty is a qualitative editorial judgment, not a measured performance claim.

This is a single-node standalone case. The presentation supplies a named 45-year-old woman and clinic context; the current update supplies the original diagnosis, treatment, interval improvement and present recurrence. No prior scored answer, prior feedback or later result is needed to solve it. No exhibit is supplied or promised. No multi-part continuity defect applies.

Scope: this report evaluates the latest candidate for each of the two salvage case lines requested by the user, replacing the historical recurrent-clearance v2 node with current v3 for review. claims.limitation: No new ABI cutoff or compression strength is authored.

claims.statement: ESVS advises against sustained ulcer compression when ankle pressure is below 60 mm Hg, toe pressure below 30 mm Hg, or ABI below 0.6.

claims.statement: Compression supports healing in an assessed venous ulcer with adequate arterial perfusion.

claims.statement: ESVS allows consideration of closely supervised modified compression below 40 mm Hg in selected mixed ulcers when ankle pressure exceeds 60 mm Hg; its discussion also uses toe pressure above 30 mm Hg and ABI above 0.6.
claims.limitation: Lower-strength recommendation 74 and section 6.3.3; one directly retrieved guideline for this exact boundary. Borderline/disputed ranges withheld.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the explicitly stated ulcer and ipsilateral arterial findings.

claims.statement: For an appropriately assessed active venous ulcer, ESVS recommends multilayer/inelastic compression or adjustable garments targeting at least 40 mm Hg at the ankle.

claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the explicitly stated ulcer and ipsilateral arterial findings.

claims.statement: Compression eligibility must use current affected-limb perfusion rather than another limb or an unreconciled old measurement.
claims.limitation: Application of physiology and eligible compression populations, not a performance estimate.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no pediatric, pregnancy or universal prescribing extrapolation.

claims.statement: A negative initial proximal ultrasound with continuing intermediate or high suspicion and no alternative diagnosis can require serial proximal ultrasound.
claims.limitation: No exact repeat interval is taught in these drafts.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no pediatric, pregnancy or universal prescribing extrapolation.

claims.statement: A technically limited or wrong-territory venous examination cannot establish absence of thrombosis in unexamined proximal segments.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no pediatric, pregnancy or universal prescribing extrapolation.

claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the exact stated scenario; no universal dose or procedure ranking.

claims.statement: New cannulation difficulty, reduced dialysis delivery, prolonged post-needle bleeding or arm swelling warrant access evaluation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no universal dose or procedure ranking.

claims.statement: A prior neuropathic hand diagnosis does not remove the need to assess a new dialysis-access-related perfusion presentation; carpal tunnel and other nonvascular causes remain competing explanations.

claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no pediatric, pregnancy or universal prescribing extrapolation.

claims.limitation: One adequate guideline; rare complication and overlapping causes require urgent vascular examination.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no universal dose or procedure ranking.

claims.statement: Suspected ischemic monomelic neuropathy after access formation requires urgent surgical assessment for access closure rather than delayed electrodiagnostic confirmation.
claims.limitation: Guideline describes immediate ligation; not every postoperative neuropathy requires ligation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no universal dose or procedure ranking.

claims.statement: A thrombolytic lock is an initial treatment for established dialysis-catheter intraluminal dysfunction after mechanical causes have been assessed.
claims.limitation: No dose or dwell duration; trained dialysis staff, not clinic manipulation. One current guideline.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no universal dose or procedure ranking.

claims.statement: The right internal jugular route is generally favored for a tunneled dialysis catheter, avoiding subclavian access when suitable alternatives exist.
claims.limitation: Vessel patency, future access and individual anatomy can modify the default.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the stated scenario; no universal dose or procedure ranking.

claims.statement: Timed barium esophagography is the ACG first-line objective assessment for persistent or recurrent symptoms after definitive achalasia treatment.
claims.limitation: ACG names the first-line role. Seoul independently supports outcome assessment. Other findings remain complementary.

claims.statement: A standardized upright timed barium examination assesses esophageal clearance.
claims.limitation: Individual series are constructed and interpreted with symptoms and anatomy.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.

claims.statement: A barium tablet can add evidence about junction-level obstruction during esophagography.
claims.limitation: One directly checked guideline. No tablet-size or treatment cutoff authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.

claims.statement: Reliable manometric interpretation depends on junction-crossing acquisition and an adequate separated-swallow protocol.
claims.limitation: Failed studies have several completion or complementary options.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.
claims.verificationLocator: CCv4 standard protocol and ACG obstructive-symptom evaluation

claims.statement: Achalasia treatment reduces junction resistance while loss of normal motor function can persist.
claims.limitation: Improved relaxation does not establish normal bolus emptying.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG treatment goals and Seoul disease definition

claims.statement: Recurrent symptoms after myotomy can arise from residual obstruction, altered anatomy, reflux injury or persistent motor dysfunction.
claims.limitation: One directly checked guideline. Symptoms do not establish which mechanism is active.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.

claims.statement: Post-POEM symptoms require objective assessment because reflux and impaired-clearance symptoms can overlap.
claims.limitation: Endoscopy and clearance findings answer complementary questions.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in outpatient foregut assessment or clinic review of outside treatment records.
claims.verificationLocator: SAGES KQ1 and ACG post-therapy assessment

claims.statement: Endoscopy can evaluate reflux injury and luminal narrowing when symptoms recur after achalasia treatment.
claims.limitation: One directly checked guideline supports this complementary role. The current comparison uses its first-line timed-barium recommendation for recurrent retention-like symptoms.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults undergoing assessment of post-myotomy symptoms or appropriate esophageal testing.
claims.verificationLocator: ACG diagnostic testing and post-therapy assessment

claims.statement: Symptomatic spontaneous venous glucose below 54 mg/dL with symptom relief after correction supports PBH after alternative causes are evaluated.
claims.limitation: The threshold is the guideline's pragmatic criterion; postmeal timing and surgical history do not exclude all other causes.

claims.statement: CGM readings do not by themselves establish the diagnosis of PBH.
claims.limitation: Does not deny a role for CGM in education or ongoing management.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed bariatric clinic or outside-record-review context; each question supplies procedure and care phase.
claims.supportLocator: Relevant named clinical section; independently synthesized atomic fact

claims.statement: The 2024 Society for Endocrinology guideline advises against OGTT or mixed-meal provocation for PBH diagnosis.
claims.limitation: Older ESPEN/UEG and dumping guidance differ on provocation. This packet does not make a general claim for all dumping syndromes.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed bariatric clinic or outside-record-review context; each question supplies procedure and care phase.

claims.statement: Supervised fasting evaluation can be used to recreate a suspected fasting hypoglycemic syndrome when a spontaneous episode cannot be characterized.
claims.limitation: Older professional summary is a limited cross-check of a real competing test. It does not establish that unconfirmed overnight CGM readings warrant a fast or that mixed-meal testing is recommended for PBH. No duration/protocol cutoff is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed post-bariatric clinic or outside-record review; the individual vignette supplies procedure and current care phase.
claims.supportLocator: Professional summary, investigation and assay timing sections

claims.statement: Acarbose is a first pharmacological option when PBH needs drug treatment.
claims.limitation: One directly read guideline; no universal dose, efficacy probability or mandatory time-to-failure is asserted.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed bariatric clinic or outside-record-review context; each question supplies procedure and care phase.

claims.statement: Acarbose can cause abdominal pain, bloating, flatulence and diarrhea that limit continued use.
claims.limitation: No adverse-event frequency, mandatory trial duration or maximum-tolerated dose is invented; the case supplies its own withdrawal/rechallenge observations.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed post-bariatric clinic or outside-record review; the individual vignette supplies procedure and current care phase.

claims.statement: Short-acting subcutaneous octreotide or pasireotide are options when acarbose is ineffective or not tolerated.
claims.limitation: Named alternatives are not ranked against each other. No off-label prescribing approval or regimen is conferred.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed bariatric clinic or outside-record-review context; each question supplies procedure and care phase.

claims.statement: The 2024 PBH guideline places diazoxide as a possible third-line option when somatostatin analogues are not tolerated.
claims.limitation: Single guideline, recommendation 3.3; no dose or eligibility protocol authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed bariatric clinic or outside-record-review context; each question supplies procedure and care phase.

claims.statement: Conventional delayed-release PPI administration should be checked relative to meals; ACG recommends dosing 30-60 minutes before a meal rather than at bedtime.
claims.limitation: Applies to conventional delayed-release preparations such as the named omeprazole, not every formulation. This medication interval is directly sourced and is not a gameplay wait.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed post-bariatric clinic or outside-record review; the individual vignette supplies procedure and current care phase.
claims.supportLocator: ACG PPI administration and optimization sections

claims.statement: PPI adherence and administration should be assessed and optimized before labeling persistent symptoms treatment-refractory.
claims.limitation: SAGES supplies the post-sleeve medical-first setting; ACG provides the administration check. No universal dose, maximum regimen or mandatory treatment duration is invented.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed post-bariatric clinic or outside-record review; the individual vignette supplies procedure and current care phase.
claims.supportLocator: ACG refractory GERD recommendations and optimization; SAGES KQ2

claims.statement: For established GERD with persistent symptoms on twice-daily PPI, ACG recommends impedance-pH monitoring on therapy to evaluate the ongoing symptoms.
claims.limitation: The question supplies prior LA grade C esophagitis and a recorded twice-daily regimen. This does not diagnose recurrent reflux from symptoms or claim every symptom is reflux-mediated.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed post-bariatric clinic or outside-record review; the individual vignette supplies procedure and current care phase.
claims.supportLocator: ACG refractory GERD recommendations and reflux monitoring section

claims.statement: Off-therapy reflux monitoring is used to establish GERD when prior objective evidence has not established the diagnosis.
claims.limitation: Contrasts diagnostic confirmation with investigation of symptoms in already established disease. Severe LA C/D esophagitis is prior objective evidence; no new acid-exposure cutoff is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed post-bariatric clinic or outside-record review; the individual vignette supplies procedure and current care phase.

claims.statement: Impedance-pH monitoring can relate symptoms to nonacid as well as acid reflux, whereas pH-only monitoring does not capture the full nonacid question during PPI therapy.
claims.limitation: One society guideline; no diagnostic yield, sensitivity, prevalence or symptom-association cutoff is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed post-bariatric clinic or outside-record review; the individual vignette supplies procedure and current care phase.

claims.statement: Unfavorable ultrasound findings such as trapped fluid can predict more difficult reduction without independently prohibiting enema reduction in a stable child without peritonitis or perforation.
claims.limitation: No pressure, success probability or fixed number of attempts authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable children with ileocolic intussusception.

claims.statement: A delayed repeat image-guided enema is a reasonable option after partial reduction when the child remains stable and lacks peritoneal signs.
claims.limitation: Conditional and locally determined; no mandatory waiting interval.
claims.applicablePopulation: Children with partial progress during initial reduction.

claims.statement: Persistently symptomatic intussusception that remains unreduced after reasonable enema attempts requires operative assessment; a documented lead point strengthens that need.
claims.limitation: Recurrence alone is not a contraindication to another enema. Operation is keyed for persistent failed reduction plus a structural lesion, not age alone.
claims.applicablePopulation: Persistent or recurrent ileocolic intussusception.

claims.statement: Transient small-bowel intussusception that resolves clinically and on reassessment differs from persistent symptomatic ileocolic intussusception.
claims.limitation: The authored case has residual ileocolic disease; no length cutoff or automatic observation rule.
claims.applicablePopulation: Children with transient small-bowel invagination.

claims.statement: A fixed bowel loop should be interpreted with the infant's overall course rather than treated as an independent absolute indication for NEC surgery.
claims.limitation: Conditional recommendation, very-low certainty. No reassuring inference from absence of free air alone.
claims.applicablePopulation: Premature infants with NEC.

claims.statement: Peritoneal drainage can serve as a bridge when early NEC operation is not possible, and deterioration after drainage may still require laparotomy.
claims.limitation: Many require later laparotomy; exact rescue thresholds are not defined.
claims.applicablePopulation: Premature infants with suspected or confirmed perforated NEC.

claims.statement: Initial laparotomy and initial drainage are both reasonable approaches to perforated NEC depending on patient and center factors.
claims.limitation: No universal superiority claim; the authored later deterioration is distinct from initial procedural choice.
claims.applicablePopulation: Premature neonates with perforated NEC.

claims.statement: Inspissated meconium in the distal ileum can cause neonatal bowel obstruction and warrants cystic-fibrosis evaluation.
claims.limitation: Meconium ileus is not itself proof of cystic fibrosis.
claims.applicablePopulation: Neonates with meconium ileus.

claims.statement: Selected stable infants with uncomplicated meconium ileus can undergo image-guided water-soluble contrast enema after resuscitation.
claims.limitation: Single adequate systematic review; nonstandard practice. No contrast product, concentration, dose or attempt count keyed.
claims.applicablePopulation: Resuscitated stable infants without perforation or other operative complications.

claims.statement: Repeat image-guided contrast enemas can decompress selected uncomplicated meconium ileus; persistent obstruction after a first attempt does not by itself define failure of the whole nonoperative course.
claims.limitation: Single adequate licensed systematic review with heterogeneous protocols; it does not establish a universal attempt count, interval, contrast preparation or obligatory repeat instead of surgery.
claims.applicablePopulation: Neonates or children in the exact constructed vignette; no universal protocol.

claims.statement: Perforation, volvulus or failed nonoperative decompression changes the operative boundary in meconium ileus.
claims.limitation: Specific operative reconstruction depends on anatomy and clinical condition.
claims.applicablePopulation: Infants with complicated or non-resolving meconium ileus.

claims.statement: For presumed Wilms tumor with caval tumor extension at or above the hepatic veins, a biopsy and preoperative chemotherapy pathway is suggested before resection.
claims.limitation: NCI professional evidence summary, not a formal COG protocol document. Exact multidisciplinary plan and biopsy technique require clinician review; no regimen or response threshold is specified.
claims.applicablePopulation: Children with presumed Wilms tumor in the stated COG/North American treatment context.

claims.statement: Bilateral disease or tumor thrombus reaching the hepatic-vein level can alter the up-front nephrectomy pathway.
claims.limitation: Counterfactual only; no drug regimen or automatic transplant/nephron-sparing technique.
claims.applicablePopulation: Wilms tumor operative planning.

claims.statement: Preoperative biopsy of an otherwise resectable Wilms tumor can assign local stage III under COG staging.
claims.limitation: Does not imply biopsy is forbidden for inoperable or atypical masses.
claims.applicablePopulation: COG-treated Wilms tumor.

claims.statement: Under the COG/North American pathway, a typical resectable unilateral Wilms tumor is generally managed with up-front nephrectomy rather than preoperative biopsy.
claims.limitation: Do not generalize to SIOP, bilateral tumors, atypical appearance, high caval extension or unsafe resection. One government evidence summary checked.
claims.applicablePopulation: Typical unilateral resectable renal tumors in a COG-aligned center.

claims.statement: Preterm inguinal-hernia timing balances incarceration during delay against respiratory and recurrence complications associated with earlier repair.
claims.limitation: Predominantly retrospective synthesis; not an absolute repair-age rule. Other 2025 syntheses differ on the incarceration estimate.
claims.applicablePopulation: Preterm infants with inguinal hernia during initial hospitalization.

claims.statement: For a reducible hernia in a very preterm infant with ongoing respiratory disease, planning repair after the initial neonatal hospitalization can be reasonable with surgical follow-up and incarceration precautions.
claims.limitation: One adequately licensed directly read synthesis. Clinical timing needs named review; no fixed postmenstrual age, weight or deadline is taught.
claims.applicablePopulation: Reducible inguinal hernia with neonatal respiratory comorbidity.
